summary: A federal republic made up of 50 states, which declared independence from Britain in 1776; it is the world's largest economy, and its diverse immigrant culture, technology and popular culture influence the whole world.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: From the 17th century, Puritans and other Protestant emigrants fleeing the pressure of the Church of England founded colonies in New England, and Protestantism thus became the mainstream faith at the nation's founding. The revivals of the "Great Awakenings" in the 18th and 19th centuries let Baptists and Methodists expand rapidly in the South and West, and Black churches also played a central role under slavery and in the civil rights movement. The share has declined in recent decades, mainly toward the religiously unaffiliated.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Before the 1990s, fewer than one in ten Americans identified as having no religion, but the number has since grown rapidly: the younger generation's aversion to the religious right's involvement in politics, the exposure from 2002 of Catholic clergy sexual abuse scandals, rising educational levels and the diversity of information in the internet age have all led many people to leave churches. Most of these "nones" still believe in some kind of spirituality but no longer identify with any denomination, and their share is highest on the West Coast, in the Northeast and among younger people.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Maryland colony, founded in 1634, had providing refuge for Catholics as one of its purposes, but Catholics remained a minority throughout the colonial period. The Irish famine of the 1840s and later waves of German, Italian and Polish immigrants made Catholicism the largest single denomination in the United States, and also provoked anti-Catholic movements such as the "Know-Nothing" party of the 1850s. In 1960 Kennedy became the first Catholic president, and in recent years Catholic growth has come mainly from Latin American immigrants.

ranking.name: Other Christian groups (Mormons, Eastern Orthodox, etc.)
ranking.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) was founded by Joseph Smith in New York State in 1830; its followers, persecuted, moved west and arrived in Utah in 1847 under Brigham Young, and Utah remains predominantly Mormon today. Eastern Orthodoxy entered Alaska with Russian missionaries in the late 18th century and was brought by Greek, Russian, Ukrainian and other immigrants in the 19th and 20th centuries.

ranking.name: Judaism
ranking.description: In 1654 the first Sephardic Jews arrived in Dutch-ruled New Amsterdam (now New York). German Jews immigrated in the 19th century, and between 1880 and 1924 about two million Eastern European Jews came to the United States to escape persecution, most settling in New York. Refugees fleeing the Nazis arrived around the time of the Second World War, making the United States the site of the largest Jewish community in the world outside Israel.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Some of the African slaves trafficked to the Americas were originally Muslims, but their faith was difficult to sustain under slavery. African American movements of the 20th century such as the "Nation of Islam" attracted people such as Malcolm X, and after the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act abolished national-origin quotas, large numbers of Muslims from the Middle East, South Asia and Africa immigrated to the United States, mainly concentrated in large cities.

religion.background: The Native American peoples originally had their own religious traditions. From the 17th century English colonists brought a variety of Protestant denominations, and many came to escape religious persecution, making religious freedom a founding ideal; the First Amendment of the Constitution in 1791 prohibits Congress from establishing a state religion. Large-scale immigration in the 19th and 20th centuries brought Catholicism, Judaism and Eastern Orthodoxy, and after 1965 brought Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism. In recent decades the Christian share has declined and the non-religious population has grown rapidly.

language.official: English is the official language (designated by presidential executive order in 2025; federal law does not explicitly provide for it), and has long been the de facto national language.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: After the founding of Jamestown in 1607 and the Plymouth Colony in 1620, English became the main language of the British North American colonies. After the founding of the nation, public schools and immigrant assimilation policies led German, Italian and other immigrant languages to give way to English within two or three generations; in 1828 Noah Webster published his dictionary, establishing American spelling. English is therefore the mother tongue of the great majority of Americans and the common language across the country.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: The southwestern United States was formerly Spanish colonial territory and then Mexican, and was incorporated into the United States after the Mexican-American War of 1848, so there were already Spanish-speaking residents there. Large-scale immigration from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba and Central America since the second half of the 20th century has made Spanish the second most widely spoken language, concentrated in California, Texas, Florida and New York.

ranking.name: Chinese
ranking.description: The California Gold Rush of 1849 attracted large numbers of Cantonese migrants, and the earliest Chinese-speaking communities mainly spoke Cantonese, but the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 restricted Chinese immigration for sixty years and was not repealed until 1943. After the immigration law reform of 1965, immigration from Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China grew greatly; Chinese speakers are concentrated in San Francisco, New York and Los Angeles, and the share of Mandarin has gradually surpassed that of Cantonese.

ranking.name: Tagalog
ranking.description: The Philippines was a U.S. colony from 1898 to 1946, and the two countries have close ties. After the 1965 immigration reform, American hospitals recruited large numbers of Filipino nurses, and together with family reunification immigration this made Tagalog one of the main Asian languages in the United States, with speakers concentrated in California and Hawaii.

ranking.name: Vietnamese
ranking.description: After the fall of Saigon in 1975, large numbers of South Vietnamese refugees and later "boat people" settled in the United States as refugees, forming the Vietnamese American community. They are concentrated in places such as "Little Saigon" in Orange County, California, and Houston, Texas, and Vietnamese has been preserved in homes, churches and shops, becoming one of the main immigrant languages in the United States.

language.history: Native North Americans originally spoke hundreds of languages, and colonization and assimilation policies caused many to disappear or become endangered. English colonization in the 17th century brought English, while Dutch, French, Spanish and German were also spoken in different regions at the same time. After the nation's founding, English dominated education and government, and European immigrants of the 19th and 20th centuries switched to English within a few generations. After the 1965 immigration reform, immigration from Latin America and Asia grew greatly and Spanish became the second most widely spoken language; a 2025 presidential executive order designated English as the official language for the first time.

ranking.name: Hamburger
ranking.description: Two round buns sandwich a fried or grilled ground beef patty, served with lettuce, tomato, onion, cheese, ketchup and mustard, often accompanied by french fries.
ranking.history: In the 19th century German immigrants brought the "Hamburg steak," popular in the port of Hamburg, to the United States; in the early 20th century restaurants everywhere began putting the patty in a bun, with places such as Connecticut and Wisconsin all claiming to be the birthplace, and the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair also made it famous. In 1921 White Castle pioneered the hamburger fast-food chain, and in the 1950s McDonald's took the hamburger across the country and the world with standardized production and a franchise model. The hamburger has thus become a symbol of American car and fast-food culture.

ranking.name: Hot dog
ranking.description: A boiled or grilled long sausage is placed in a long soft bun and topped with mustard and ketchup, then onions, pickle relish or sauerkraut.
ranking.history: In the mid-19th century German immigrants brought the frankfurter sausage to the United States, and in the 1870s sausage stands selling sausages in buns appeared on Coney Island in New York. The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago and professional baseball parks made the hot dog a convenient everyday food to eat on the move; the term "hot dog" became popular in college newspapers around the 1890s. In 1939 President Roosevelt served hot dogs to King George VI of Britain, and hot dogs have since been regarded as a representative American food, an indispensable part of Independence Day cookouts.

ranking.name: American barbecue
ranking.description: Pork, brisket and ribs are slow-cooked or smoked for hours at low temperature over wood or charcoal, then served with sauces, breads and slaws that differ in style from region to region.
ranking.history: The word "barbecue" comes from "barbacoa" (a wooden frame set over a fire) of the Taíno people of the Caribbean and was brought to North America by the Spanish. In the colonial period the South focused on slow-roasting whole hogs, and many pitmasters were enslaved Africans whose skills established the Southern barbecue tradition. Styles later developed in different places, such as vinegar-sauced pulled pork in the Carolinas, brisket in Texas influenced by German and Czech immigrants, and sweet-sauced ribs in Kansas City; Independence Day and summer backyard cookouts are important social events for Americans.

ranking.name: Southern fried chicken
ranking.description: Chicken pieces are marinated in spices, coated in flour and fried in oil until the skin is golden and crisp and the meat juicy, often served with biscuits and gravy.
ranking.history: Southern fried chicken combined the frying methods of Scottish immigrants with West African seasoning traditions, and took shape during the colonial period in plantations through the work of enslaved African American cooks. After emancipation, African American women in places such as Virginia sold fried chicken to passengers at railway stations as a way of making a living. In 1952 Colonel Sanders began promoting "Kentucky Fried Chicken" through franchising, taking fried chicken across the country and around the world, and it remains a classic dish of the Southern Sunday family dinner.

ranking.name: Apple pie
ranking.description: Sliced apples, sugar, cinnamon and a little lemon juice are enclosed in a buttery pastry and baked, the top often a lattice or a full crust, and it is often served with vanilla ice cream.
ranking.history: Apples are not native to North America; in the 17th century English colonists brought apple seeds and grafting wood to the New World, and the method of making apple pie originated in England, with the earliest recipes traceable to the 14th century. In the early 19th century John Chapman ("Johnny Appleseed") raised large numbers of seedlings in the Midwest, spreading apple trees across the United States with the pioneers. During the Second World War, American soldiers often said they were fighting for "mom and apple pie," and "as American as apple pie" has become a saying for describing something authentically American.
